name: Jade Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What is a usual shift like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and a junior agent on Sunday calls and chats at the contact centre. I finished secondary school and came here after an alterations shop closed. I use the approved AI sorter every day to pull a customer’s latest return request from a long chat, but I still miss exceptions that a senior agent catches. The Sunday premium makes my pay higher than most agents even though I am still learning.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is there outside the Sunday queue?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Rui repairs bicycles, and our grown children have their own homes. We rent and have about eleven months of expenses saved; several other centres are close enough to reach by bus. I still mend clothes for family because I enjoy seeing a torn seam hold again, but I have not charged anyone for that work. I can picture fewer paid shifts someday, yet Rui and I have no settled replacement income or retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the Sunday desk AI Plateau is close to the sorter I already use: it finds the latest return request, then a person checks the refund. I would keep the account page open beside it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my Sunday shifts stay busy in this picture. Eleven months saved makes an unexpected rent rise less frightening, though I am still the junior who asks for help on odd returns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep answering return chats and checking the AI sorter against the actual refund page. In the first year of small change, I’d ask a senior agent to walk through one returned-but-unpaid parcel with me on a paid shift each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about earnings, curious about the exceptions. A parcel marked received is not the same as money returned to a card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which return fooled the sorter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A customer sent a coat back, but the sorter picked the warehouse scan as if it were a refund. The senior agent showed me the empty payment field before I replied.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the reserve for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rui (my partner) and I can leave our eleven-month reserve for real gaps. I would not call a faster sorter an extra wage.

think: I think my **Sunday shifts** stay busy.
I know **eleven months saved** eases a rent shock.
I still need **senior help** on unusual returns.

Ask a **senior agent** to coach one unpaid-return case monthly on a paid shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption could answer the plain return questions and leave the Sunday agents with missing payments. I would ask the supervisor for a paid rota alongside the new system’s error count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my premium shifts could be cut even if I learn the tool faster than some colleagues. Eleven months saved means I can refuse an unpaid “opportunity” and keep looking for real paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d learn the new return-audit tool by running twenty old missing-refund cases through it on a paid shift if wrong answers can be logged. In the first year routine chats move, I’d stay on my paid Sunday rota while comparing actual errors with lost hours and ask the supervisor to explain any cut in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the rota, keen to see what the tool misses. A machine can close a return quickly and leave a customer waiting for money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the audit count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count cases where the parcel arrived but the refund did not. A chart of fast closures is not useful without the missing payments beside it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take unpaid trial work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put my old and new Sunday rotas side by side before changing anything. Rui (my partner) and I have time to compare, so I will not accept free trial work as a replacement wage.

I’d warn **plain returns** may move before missing refunds do.
think: I think my **premium shifts** could shrink.
I can reject **unpaid offers** because the reserve gives us time.
do: Test **twenty missing refunds** with the new audit tool on paid time only if wrong answers can be logged.
Keep **paid Sunday shifts** and compare old/new rosters with errors; ask for any cut in writing.
feel: **Anxious** about paid hours, keen to measure errors.

fieldNote: The **new audit test** is distinct from daily sorter use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the Sunday team AGI by 2028 could settle almost every ordinary return before I open a chat. I would ask for written Sunday-hour notice and a real way customers can challenge wrong refunds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the premium shifts could go in 2028. Robots around 2031 may later reach hands-on repair work, but eleven months saved gives me a chance to find out whether people will pay for mending now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d tell three neighbours I can repair zips and hems for a posted small fee, take only jobs my home sewing machine can handle, and record what each job earns. In the first year after 2028, if Sunday hours fall, I’d use no more than one month of our existing savings to buy basic thread and travel to paying customers; I’d offer two paid mending afternoons a week only if the first three jobs cover their materials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried about the shift, willing to test a small trade I know. A jar of thread cannot replace a Sunday wage until someone actually pays for a repaired coat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which repairs would you take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would start with ordinary hems and working zips, not promise leather repairs I cannot do. A return customer paying for a second repair would tell me more than a friendly compliment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much reserve would you risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rui (my partner) and I would keep the rest of the reserve for rent. Our grown children can bring clothes to mend, but I would not count free family repairs as sales.

I’d warn **2028 AGI** could settle ordinary returns.
think: I think my **premium shifts** could go in 2028.
I can test **paid mending** using a bounded part of existing savings.
do: Offer **zip and hem repairs** to three neighbours for posted fees in 2026 only within home-machine capacity; record earnings.
If Sunday hours fall after 2028, spend at most **one month** of existing savings on thread and customer travel.
Offer **two paid mending afternoons** weekly only if three early jobs cover their materials.
feel: **Worried** about shifts, willing to test a familiar trade.
S2.quote: A jar of thread cannot replace a Sunday wage until someone actually pays for a repaired coat.
fieldNote: The **eleven-month reserve** funds a capped experiment, not a full wage.
She prices **real neighbours’ repairs** rather than counting free family work.
She knows **2031 robots** may later reach physical repair tasks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives me time to see whether a small paid repair service can stand beside my call wage. I would ask the centre to publish Sunday hours early so I can plan the other work honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years is enough to improve a trade I used to do, though robots around 2034 may later reach hands-on repairs. I can afford one modest course fee from eleven months saved, but I will not quit paid calls on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’d enroll in a weekend upholstery-repair course only if the fee stays below one week of my usual pay and classes do not replace paid Sunday shifts. In the first year after 2031, if call hours fall, I’d take paid chair-cover and zip jobs on two afternoons only when the price covers materials and travel, while keeping any paid calls that remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Curious about making the old skill earn again, uneasy about counting on it too soon. A repaired chair is a business only when a stranger pays the agreed price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the course teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would practise on a torn chair cover before charging anyone. A trainer should tell me which seams will hold and which jobs I must refuse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must remain in savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show Rui (my partner) the course fee and our remaining reserve before enrolling. We would keep enough cash for at least six months of rent after paying for the class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives time to build a repair ledger while the Sunday queue still pays. I would ask for yearly paid-hour figures so no one has to guess when calls are shrinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could keep earning for years and learn whether neighbours return for paid repairs. Eleven months saved helps me try; it is not a pension or a promise that I can stop full-time work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep paid Sunday calls and offer one paid sewing afternoon monthly, writing down receipts and material costs. In the first year after 2036, if call hours fall, I’d expand to two paid repair afternoons only after six consecutive months of receipts cover their own costs and part of our rent; otherwise I’d keep whichever calls remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cautious, with time to see real numbers. Ten years before AGI reaches my calls is time to earn a second ledger, not time to write a retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the ledger count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count repeat paying customers, not pieces I mend for relatives. The notebook has to show what came in after thread, bus fare and the hours I spent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you reduce call hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rui (my partner) and I would decide about fewer Sunday calls only when the household budget works without them. Our grown children have separate bills, and the plan does not use their wages.

I’d build a **repair ledger** while Sunday calls still pay.

I will not treat **eleven months saved** as retirement income.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it could do the easy return chats that fill my Sunday shifts. Eleven months saved gives us space to try paid mending without taking the first weak job offer, but that reserve is finite. Written notice of Sunday hours and clear rules for customers to appeal wrong machine returns would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask what a customer does when a returned parcel is marked received but never refunded. A returned coat cannot pay for the replacement until somebody finds the missing money.

headlineQuote: A returned coat cannot pay for the replacement until somebody finds the missing money.
portrait: At **58**, Jade is a junior agent after secondary school and alterations-shop work.
She and Rui rent with **eleven months saved** and a higher Sunday premium.
She uses **AI daily** but still needs help with return exceptions.
She can test **paid sewing repairs** while continuing call shifts.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove the easy Sunday return chats that pay her premium.
whatWouldHelp: **Written Sunday-hour notice** and a clear customer appeal route would help.
